title: Trump Rejects Iran’s Truce Offer: Inside the “Better Deal” Strategy Unveiled by Al Jazeera
body:
Washington’s top diplomat has turned down Iran’s latest overture to halt hostilities in the Gulf and reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a move that analysts say reflects President Donald Trump’s belief that sustained economic pressure will extract deeper concessions from Tehran. The decision, announced on Monday, comes amid a fragile cease‑fire that has held for just over a week and a flurry of diplomatic activity involving regional powers and European mediators.

Trump’s rejection hinges on a calculation that the United States can leverage its extensive sanctions regime to force Iran into a more comprehensive settlement. The Iranian proposal, presented through back‑channel contacts, offered an immediate cessation of missile strikes on oil facilities and a pledge to keep the Hormuz shipping lane open for commercial traffic. In return, Tehran sought the lifting of a series of U.S. sanctions targeting its oil exports, banking sector, and key individuals. While the offer addressed the most urgent security concerns, it fell short of Iran’s broader demand for a full rollback of the sanctions that have crippled its economy since 2018.

Experts warn that the president’s hard‑line stance may be a double‑edged sword. “Sanctions have been the centerpiece of U.S. policy toward Iran for years, and Trump sees them as the primary bargaining chip,” said Dr. Lila Mahmoud, a senior fellow at the Center for Middle East Policy. “But the longer the sanctions stay in place, the more Tehran can claim they are bearing the brunt of American aggression, which could erode U.S. credibility and limit future diplomatic options.” The administration’s approach also risks alienating allies such as the United Kingdom and France, who have been pushing for a multilateral framework that couples sanctions relief with verifiable limits on Iran’s ballistic‑missile program.

Regional dynamics add another layer of complexity. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, wary of Iran’s growing influence, have welcomed the cease‑fire but remain skeptical of any deal that does not curb Tehran’s missile capabilities. Meanwhile, Israel has openly criticized Washington’s willingness to negotiate, warning that a premature settlement could embolden Iran’s regional proxies. The divergent priorities of these stakeholders make it difficult for the United States to present a unified front, increasing the likelihood that negotiations will stall unless a broader coalition can be forged.

The economic calculus behind Trump’s decision also reflects domestic political considerations. With the 2024 election looming, the president has repeatedly framed Iran as a national security threat, using the conflict to rally his base. By maintaining pressure, Trump hopes to portray himself as the defender of American interests abroad, a narrative that resonates with his supporters. However, critics argue that this strategy may backfire if the conflict escalates, potentially disrupting global oil markets and inflating gasoline prices at a time when many Americans are already feeling economic strain.

Looking ahead, the United States appears poised to continue its “maximum pressure” campaign, but the window for diplomatic resolution may be narrowing. Analysts suggest that if Tehran perceives the sanctions as an existential threat, it could resort to more aggressive actions, such as targeting additional shipping lanes or expanding its missile strikes. Conversely, a sustained stalemate could push moderate voices within Iran’s political elite to seek a negotiated settlement, especially if the economic toll becomes unbearable. The coming weeks will test whether Washington’s gamble on sanctions will yield the desired leverage or push the region toward a deeper, more volatile confrontation.
